analysis.one_liner: Requires big political spenders—corporations, unions, super PACs, and nonprofits—to disclose their donors and blocks foreign-controlled corporations from election spending.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 45 Senate cosponsors on top of the sponsor, the bill was sent to the Rules Committee, never got a hearing or vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required any corporation, labor union, super PAC, or tax-exempt group that spends more than $10,000 on campaign ads to report its major funders to the Federal Election Commission, including the people behind shell entities. It would also tighten the existing ban on foreign money in elections, covering domestic corporations that are owned or steered by foreign interests, and require CEOs to certify compliance under penalty of perjury. In short: before an ad asks you to vote for or against a candidate, you would be able to see who paid for it.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would learn the identities of the people and companies funding campaign ads before they vote. Small donors and grassroots groups also gain, because they compete on a more level field when large anonymous spenders must stand behind their ads. Candidates and officeholders would face less pressure from undisclosed spenders.

how_it_helps.text: Any covered organization spending more than $10,000 in an election cycle would have to file a statement within 24 hours of crossing that threshold, listing each payment over $1,000 and the name and address of every person who gave $10,000 or more toward the spending.

Groups would have to name their beneficial owners—the actual people who control them or profit from them—so that money routed through LLCs, trusts, or nonprofits could not be laundered into anonymity.

The bill extends the existing ban on foreign-national contributions to domestic corporations that are foreign-owned or foreign-controlled, and requires corporate CEOs to certify annually under penalty of perjury that their political spending complies.

It broadens what counts as an election ad: the 'functional equivalent of express advocacy' standard and an expanded electioneering-communication window (starting January 1 of the election year for most races) mean more ads fall under disclosure rules instead of slipping through as 'issue' ads.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, labor unions, super PACs, and tax-exempt groups that spend on elections would bear new reporting and compliance costs, and their donors would lose anonymity when giving toward campaign ads. Foreign-controlled corporations would lose the ability to spend at all.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporate, union, and nonprofit political spenders

drawbacks.text: Disclosure imposes real compliance burdens: covered groups must file within 24 hours, report individual payments over $1,000, and identify beneficial owners through layers of legal entities—an administrative lift that falls hardest on small nonprofits and unions rather than large corporate legal departments.

A good-faith objection to donor disclosure is that publicizing the names of givers can expose them to harassment or retaliation; the bill's carve-outs (for ordinary commercial revenue and for donors who forbid their money from being used politically in writing) reduce but do not eliminate this concern.

Expanding the electioneering-communication window to the entire election year pulls early issue advocacy—ads on policy that merely mention a candidate—into campaign reporting, which critics say can chill legitimate speech about public affairs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is straightforward: voters would know who is paying for the ads trying to influence their votes, and foreign-controlled money would face a firmer ban. The costs are compliance paperwork for unions and nonprofits and reduced anonymity for donors giving toward political ads. On balance the transparency gains to voters outweigh the administrative burden, though the strongest objection—exposing donors to retaliation—deserves to be taken seriously rather than dismissed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, which never acted on it, so it quietly died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the DISCLOSE Act of 2017 on July 19, 2017, joined by 45 cosponsors (43 Democrats and 2 independents).
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration.
No further action was ever taken—no hearing, no markup, no vote—and the bill expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The organizations that spend on elections without naming their donors—corporations, trade groups, and dark-money nonprofits—kept that ability intact, because the bill never advanced. Voters never got the disclosure it promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Undisclosed political spenders kept the status quo

for.name: Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, the Senate's main campaign-disclosure measure of the Congress.

for.name: 43 of 46 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the minority and party leadership (Schumer, Durbin, Klobuchar).

for.name: 2 Independent senators
for.role: Senate cosponsors (Sanders of Vermont, King of Maine)

against.name: Roy Blunt
against.role: Chair, Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the committee took no action in the 18 months before the Congress ended.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought campaign-disclosure legislation to the Senate floor; he has long opposed mandated donor disclosure as an infringement on political speech.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or independent—46 senators in all—and no Republican signed on; with Republicans holding both the Senate majority and the Rules Committee chair, the bill never moved.

industries.industry: Corporations and trade associations that fund campaign ads
industries.note: They would have had to disclose their beneficial owners and every large donor behind their election spending within 24 hours of crossing $10,000. The bill's whole purpose was to end the anonymity under which they influence elections, so their interest in killing it ran directly against voters' interest in knowing who is paying.

These organizations are currently the main channel for anonymous political spending; the bill made them 'covered organizations' required to name their donors and owners. Their business model depends on the secrecy this bill would have removed.

The bill explicitly extended the foreign-money ban to domestic corporations steered or owned by foreign nationals, with CEO certifications under penalty of perjury. Their ability to shape U.S. elections through domestic subsidiaries would have been cut off.

Unions are covered by the same disclosure requirements as corporations, a symmetry the bill's drafters built in deliberately. Unions had little to gain from the foreign-money provisions but shared the compliance burden of donor and disbursement reporting.

Super PACs already report most donors, but the bill required reporting of 'covered transfers'—money routed to them from nonprofits or other entities—closing the pass-through that lets donors reach them anonymously.
